what_its_for: Triptorelin is used to treat advanced prostate cancer in men. It works by lowering the amount of testosterone in your body, which helps slow down or stop the growth of prostate cancer cells. It may also be used to treat certain other hormone-related conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, or early puberty in children.
how_to_take: Triptorelin is given as an injection into your muscle (usually the buttock) by a doctor or nurse in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT inject this medication yourself at home. Your healthcare provider will give you this shot on a schedule — usually once every 1, 3, or 6 months depending on the type of triptorelin prescribed. Always keep your scheduled appointments so you do not miss a dose.
dosing: The dose and how often you receive it depends on the specific product your doctor prescribed. Common schedules include: one injection every 4 weeks (monthly), one injection every 12 weeks (every 3 months), or one injection every 24 weeks (every 6 months). Your doctor will choose the right dose and schedule for your condition. Do not try to change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because triptorelin is given by a healthcare provider, it is important to keep all of your scheduled clinic appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an injection appointment, call your doctor's office as soon as possible to reschedule. Missing doses can allow your hormone levels to rise again and may reduce how well the medication works.
storage: Triptorelin is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. You do not need to store it at home. If for any reason you are given a supply to bring to another facility, keep it at room temperature (between 20°C and 25°C or 68°F and 77°F), protected from light, and out of reach of children. Do not freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid missing your scheduled injection appointments, as this can reduce the effectiveness of your treatment. Tell your doctor before starting triptorelin if you take any other medications, including supplements and herbal products, especially medications that affect your heart rhythm (such as those for irregular heartbeat). Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or tired after your injection. Women who are or may become pregnant should not handle or receive this medication, as it can cause serious harm to an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden weakness or numbness in your arms or legs, trouble walking or loss of bladder or bowel control (which could be signs of spinal cord compression), chest pain or a fast or irregular heartbeat, severe bone pain, signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you notice: increased urination or difficulty urinating, mood changes or depression, hot flashes that are severe, joint pain or stiffness, new or worsening pain, or any other symptoms that worry you.
when_it_works: Triptorelin does not work instantly. During the first 1 to 2 weeks of treatment, testosterone levels may actually rise temporarily before they drop — this is called a 'flare.' You may notice a brief worsening of symptoms during this time. After about 2 to 4 weeks, testosterone levels should fall to very low levels. Your doctor will monitor your response with blood tests (such as PSA and testosterone levels). It may take several weeks to months before you notice an improvement in your symptoms.
special_populations: Older adults: Triptorelin is commonly used in older men with prostate cancer. Your doctor will monitor you closely for bone thinning (osteoporosis), heart-related effects, and changes in blood sugar or cholesterol. Children: Triptorelin may be used in children with early-onset puberty (central precocious puberty) under close specialist supervision. Doses are adjusted based on the child's weight. Women: Triptorelin is NOT safe during pregnancy as it can cause miscarriage or harm to the unborn baby. Women of childbearing age must use reliable non-hormonal contraception during treatment. Breastfeeding is not recommended while using triptorelin. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your doctor may need to monitor you more carefully, though dose adjustments are not routinely required.
